title: Active Argument Mapping: Reading for Structure Over Fact
summary: How 99th-percentile CAT test-takers track thesis pivots and author stance in under 3.5 minutes.

content_blocks.heading: 1. Why Passive Reading Fails in CAT & GMAT
content_blocks.body: Most aspirants read RC passages like newspaper articles—hoping that absorbing general meaning will suffice when answering questions. But CAT questions rarely test factual recall; they test structural relationships, unstated assumptions, and rhetorical pivots.
bullets: Track the author's voice vs. cited opinions: Does the author endorse the view or merely summarize it?
Highlight discourse pivots immediately: Words like "However", "Yet", and "Obscures" signal where the core thesis lives.

content_blocks.heading: 2. The Two-Pass Reading Routine
content_blocks.body: Spend 2.5 to 3 minutes on your first pass establishing paragraph functions. Do not memorize details; note where they live so you can verify them when answering specific inference questions.

title: The Anatomy of CAT Trap Options: How to Eliminate the 50-50 Choice
summary: A taxonomy of how exam convenors design seductive wrong options that fool over 60% of aspirants.

content_blocks.heading: The 4 Major Trap Archetypes
content_blocks.body: Exam designers rarely write obviously foolish options. The most dangerous distractors are 80% correct with a fatal flaw hidden in an adverb or causal verb.
bullets: Too Extreme: Uses absolute qualifiers like "wholly", "completely", or "invariably" where the author was guarded.
Causal Reversal: Changes who caused what, or attributes bad faith to a structural blind spot.
Out of Scope: Sounds scholarly and plausible in real life, but has zero textual warrant in this specific passage.
